MIDDLE EAST OIL FLOWS: With data for the first 10 days of November, we can see two trends emerging on Persian Gulf oil exports (ex Iran): 

A) After a very strong start of the month, crude oil flows are now materially lower, running about ~2.0m b/d below than full-month October (equal to 85% of pre-war levels, from 100% in October). The drop is widespread, but particularly acute for Kuwaiti flows. 

B) At the same time, exports of petroleum refined products are significantly higher than in Sep and Oct, suggesting a deliberate effort to prioritize them at the expense of crude. Kuwait and UAE are mostly behind the boost of refined products. All said, Nov 1-10 refined petroleum products exports are running at ~65% of prewar levels, up from 50%-40% in Oct-Sep.

But all together, and ex-Iran Middle East total oil flows are lower than Oct, but roughly on par with September. The composition has changed, however, with crude materially lower, and refined products materially higher.

This is not something that I'm worried about, especially since we've seen much bigger liquidation events in the past.

But this time, I'm more concerned about the negative Bitcoin ETF inflows.

$2.35B left Bitcoin ETFs in just two weeks. That's a reversal of the buying pressure that helped BTC recover earlier this year.

2. Nvidia

Nvidia dropped 13% in the past week, with BTC falling alongside it. It's not true 100% of the time, but crypto often follows big tech's moves.

3. Interest Rates

U.S. inflation is proving stubborn, and traders are betting on another Fed rate hike. As per usual, higher interest rates make assets like BTC less attractive.

4. Strategy

MSCI is removing $MSTR from its indexes. That could trigger forced stock selling and make it harder for @Strategy to raise money for more BTC purchases.

5. Liquidations

Around $1.5B was liquidated in 24 hours, compared to $19B during the Oct 2025 crash.

I don't think liquidations alone explain this selloff. We can call bottom once ETF inflows return and BTC reclaims its 200-day moving average.

Until then, be smart and protect your capital.

It appears we are still in a late stage bear cycle with depression now creeping in. Think this is evident from broader market psychology and also paying attention to my personnel psychology.

Despite clear objective breaks in bearish market structure and positive shifts in relevant trending indicators we retraced that full move and now sit at the moment where we were over summer.

Some thoughts on the market as I believe de-risking is being driven by wider market uncertainty and what I will be watching for in the coming months:

[1] The U.S. conflict with Iran sparked a global energy crisis which has been a clear inflationary pressure and now driving FED policy. Despite oil now flowing through the strait again and an aggressive sell off in oil remains one of the key points for uncertainty.

[2] The FED has now entered into a new hiking cycle which naturally contracts global liquidity as capital flows out of risk into treasuries. Bitcoin largely benefits from a positive liquidity environment and this was the main dilemma between price action and the macro backdrop.

[3] High profile IPOs like Anthropic are multiple times oversubscribed which may be acting as a liquidity sink in the interim. Driving a rotation out of BTC into new high profile tech names. UPnL from the private markets will end up being friction on the indicies over 2027.

[4] AI related advancements as it relates to cybersecurity threats and potential weaknesses in encryption are also effecting participant psychology. I think the latter is over indexed on and the former remains a very real threat. Ultimately does not instil confidence and acts as a psychological drag.

[5] Core AI equities have seen an aggressive selloff as fears arise on revenue generated from the AI build out may not meet the debt incurred from aggressive CapEx. We has Jensen outed and concerns as it relates to open source self hosted models driving more demand from token spend. Weakness perceived in frontier labs which are set to IPO.

[6] Democrats won the mid terms and uncertainty surrounding how aggressive they will be as it relates to digital asset regulatory treatment. CFTC and SEC remains incredibly positive as it relates to on shoring digital asset innovation and market leaders.

Ultimately I think there is uncertainty from numerous vectors. Price is now indicative of a depression like market environment as it relates to where we sit on the cycle. I think rates peaking will be very important as it relates to expressing positive outlook on market liquidity. Equities are still a clear friction point for any risk on behaviour in the interim.

Going against ones own psychology and wider market psychology that depression is the latest stage of a bear market cycle. In the coming months it will most likely be wise to swim against this psychology.

There is something like this every day. The contraction of onchain is sadly going to continue for a while as a result. People will rationally continue to remove funds the more they see high profile names getting scares.

I am now forced to manage the risk of how much to leave on perps dexs. 

I think once the industry demonstrates a big year on year decrease in funds lost to hackers then we will grow again. This year we have managed to lose more in hacks than onchain revenue, which is clearly insane. 

Or we somehow solve the insurance problem, which seems impossible.

A little more colour:

The extent of the recent fall has been severe, but that itself does not mean much if what is happening is a rapid repricing of tightening liquidity conditions

We have many competing forces now: strong historical support levels, 5-year CAGR approaching 2022 bottom, 11-day streak of lower highs (an all-time record today at 12 if we hold below yesterday's high), mass long liquidations, OI dominance reset etc.

But concurrently we have rapidly tightening dollar liquidity and a strong negative trend, with many, many more long liquidations piled up below

Think the most probable scenario is near-term relief here purely based on how many consecutive lower highs we've put in followed by continuation lower later this month - and that next move lower is likely where everyone entirely gives up on BTC 

Given I have now roundtripped my spot pos. back to entry I will look to buy my own blood if/when we get capitulation below 62 as I do not think this is the beginning of a secular bear + 5-year CAGR is at its most attractive from a contrarian POV + expect tightening liquidity conditions to be temporary not structural into 2027

However, the outlook for the next 13w is now pretty bleak despite the severity of the recent decline - in historical cases, despite a prior 14-day 10%+ decline, the median 13w return has been -8%, with 40% hit rate and negative skew on MFE/MAE. My systematic strategy remains flat and the BTC liquidity model I built recently also flipped to cash on Friday close (though this is not a live model unlike the systematic, just something I have been tinkering with recently)

My indicators are also approaching the buy zone again but not flashing 'BUY' yet like they did in Feb and July

Before buying my own blood, I'd want to see some combination of exhaustion in negative liquidity momentum (ROC peaks and turns) + more long liqs and persistent fear to buy the dip on perps unlike now + my systematic and/or liquidity model flipping to BUY

My own discretionary decision-making came at own detriment from a near-perfect entry to what should have been a very good exit - we all have those trades (and will continue to do so) but particularly frustrating when my own systems tell me something and I ignore thinking my discretionary view is smarter 🙃

Would argue that we’ve had plenty of sharp corrections since 2022 — they’ve just been much faster and v-bottomed — and the underlying conditions  are still not there for a 2022-esque bear market 

Liquidity has tightened at the margins but is still loose at the composite level, inflation impulses are actually contracting and growth is the puzzle piece here (if it does not crater we are absolutely fine for equities imo)

V hard to get a protracted bear in equities without a combination of rising inflation impulses (not headline prints) + contracting growth impulses + contracting liquidity momentum 

And people can talk about energy prices but Oil + Commodities 3m-12m ROC is negative and DXY is positive — that is unequivocally a disinflationary force — too much focus on absolute levels and little focus on momentum

Would definitely say the case for that weaker combination of macro impulses is stronger than it has been for a while but it’s still not there concretely 

I think the signature of Trump regimes is sharp and sporadic corrections into vol panics and v-reversals - I don’t see this changing in 2027 as it stands 

But obviously if my macro modelling starts screaming this time is actually different I will share here — not seeing anything outside of normal corrections and chop atm 

Crypto is a v different beast and extremely reliant on liquidity conditions particularly, so remains to be seen what happens there going into 2027 — but yeah what was turning into a tailwind from a dollar liquidity POV has very quickly materialised into a headwind

HYDROGRAPH: THE FIRST ORDER COULD BE THE FIRST DOMINO

#Graphene $HG.CN $HGRAF

The first major orders could be worth far more than the revenue on the invoice.

Because when a global manufacturer demonstrates a competitive advantage, every rival gets a new question:

“How much will it cost us to fall behind?”

As @iceskatergirl3 commented in the thread below, think about the competitive pressure created by the iPhone, ChatGPT or hybrid powertrains. Once an advantage becomes visible, competitors have a powerful reason to respond.

I believe people still underestimate how broadly that dynamic could apply to HydroGraph’s turbostratic Fractal Graphene.

Automotive is just one sector. Consider what could happen across these markets:

🚢 COATINGS
If better corrosion protection means fewer maintenance shutdowns for ships, bridges and industrial equipment, asset owners have a financial reason to demand it. Competing coatings suppliers then have a reason to accelerate their own testing.

🏗️ CONSTRUCTION
If a concrete producer can meet strength requirements using less cement, that could improve both costs and emissions. Rivals bidding for the same projects would have to take notice.

📦 PLASTICS & PACKAGING
If manufacturers can deliver the required strength with less material, the savings could repeat across millions of products. A small improvement per unit can become a meaningful competitive advantage at scale.

⚙️ LUBRICANTS
If reduced friction and wear translate into lower energy use, longer equipment life and less downtime, fleet managers and factory operators have a reason to ask their suppliers for the same benefits.

💻 ELECTRONICS & CONDUCTIVE MATERIALS
If producers can achieve the required conductivity with less filler, they gain another way to compete on formulation cost and performance. HydroGraph has already reported tests demonstrating that potential.
Now consider how these markets connect.

A coatings supplier may serve automotive, marine and infrastructure customers. A plastics compounder may supply packaging, electronics and industrial equipment.
One successful formulation could therefore open doors to multiple product lines, factories and industries. Meanwhile, competitors could launch their own development programmes.

That is how the domino effect could multiply: expansion within the first customer, pressure on its rivals, and introductions into adjacent markets through shared suppliers.

The scale of this opportunity is just enormous.

The first invoice would tell us what one customer bought.

It could tell us very little about how many doors that purchase might open.

But I do think the production eventually will reach much more than 50,000 metric tonnes per year with multiple production centers in Asia and Europe. I ran the numbers on BlackRock's Bitcoin ETF, and the average buyer got in around $81K.

BTC is at $65K, so they're sitting on about a 19% loss.

Yet...almost none of them have sold yet. Here's why that matters for you:

The short version: don't count on a fast recovery, don't chase bounces, and DCA monthly until the signals at the end flip.

/1 The ETF crowd hasn't sold yet

I took every day of flows into BlackRock's ETF (IBIT, by far the biggest) since launch and weighted it by that day's BTC price. 

Net inflows come out to about $80.7K'ish per BTC. 

BTC has spent most of 2026 below that line. In Sep–Oct it finally got above it, ran to about $86K, and held for a month. Then the Binance hack hit, and it fell 20%.

Since the hack, about $3B has left the spot BTC ETFs, $2.35B of it from IBIT, with outflows on 10 of the last 11 trading days.

But IBIT still holds about 795K BTC, only 4% below its peak. Most ETF holders haven't sold, instead they're sitting on a loss and waiting.

What to do: That's a lot of people who'll be tempted to sell when they get back to even. If you bought higher, don't count on a quick trip back to $81K to get out. 

If you trade, a bounce toward $81K is a place to take some profit, not to add. I'd only buy more aggressively once BTC is back above $81K and ETF flows have turned positive.

/2 Crypto's cash is shrinking

Stablecoin supply shrank by $15.5B in the last 30 days. Three quarters of that was USDT and USDC, the main dollars people use to buy crypto.

Less cash on the sidelines means fewer buyers for the dip.

The long-term picture is different. Stablecoin payments hit $482B in the first 9 months of this year, up 45% (per Allium). People are using crypto dollars more, even while they hold fewer of them.

What to do: Don't chase green days. Stick to your DCA. And watch USDT & USDC supply (free on DefiLlama). 

When it starts growing again, the buyers are coming back.

/3 Buybacks are a cushion, not a floor

At its current pace, pump is buying back about 18% of its circulating market cap a year. It's still down 35% since the hack.

Hyperliquid buys back about 5% a year, and HYPE is down 17%. That's better than BTC (-20%), ETH (-23%) & SOL (-29%).

The difference is the business behind it. Hyperliquid's buybacks over the last 30 days ran above its 12-month average. Pump ran below.

What to do: Before you buy a token for its buybacks, pull up its revenue. If the last few months are trending down, skip it, no matter how big the buyback looks.

/4 So what am I doing?

DCA monthly. At these prices, I'm happy to keep buying BTC and HYPE every month. DCA keeps it simpler than trying to time this.

Keep cash. If the selling isn't done, you'll want ammo lower.

No leverage. Not in this market, and it's not something I usually do anyway.

Be VERY Picky on alts. If I buy alts, only ones with a growing business behind the buybacks.

/5 What would tell me it's turned

USDT & USDC growing again.

ETF flows turning positive.

The Fed done hiking, and then cutting.

BTC back above $81K and holding it.

What are you doing in this market?

Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail.

At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data once, the chain learns the answer, and then we never need to see that data again. This sounds very specific, but it includes most "heavy" things happening on Ethereum:

* Signatures
* STARKs
* Merkle branches
* FHE computation
* ...

Really the first two are the most important.

Once we go quantum-safe, signatures get bigger (65 bytes ECDSA -> 1-6 kB WOTS/SPHINCS depending on params) and ZKPs get much bigger (200-1000 bytes with groth16, PLONK, etc -> 128 kB with STARKs). This is unsustainable to put on chain, and 8288 fixes this.

8288 works by aggregating STARKs in the mempool. First, you as a user generate the STARK or SPHINCS signature or PCS opening (more on that last one later), and publish it. Then, each node listens. Each tick, each node takes all of the new objects that it has seen, and generates a STARK containing a list of "claims":

"pubkey P has signed message M"
"program X run on data D has output Y"
"p(X) = Y for some polynomial P whose hash is H"

and a proof that it has seen a signature, STARK or PCS opening verifying those claims. So the only information getting re-broadcasted is:

(i) hashes of inputs and outputs (~64-96 bytes per claim)
(ii) a single STARK proof per tick

These aggregate proofs themselves get re-aggregated, and eventually you get to a single "master proof" in the block, that verifies that all of those statements are true. And so the only other data that has to actually go on chain is the statements (the (P, M), (X, D, Y), (X, Y, H) tuples I described above), not the actual signatures or proofs. This gets put into a specialized frame type.

Now, let's get into the leanSPHINCS vs leanSTARK vs leanPCS part.

The core distinction is: *what is the underlying object that the user is creating?*

In leanSPHINCS, it's a signature, and specifically this particular type of purely-hash-based signature: https://t.co/HOazliHq9N

If we add leanSPHINCS, then users will be able to make quantum-safe accounts, and pay only a little bit of gas (4096 for the 64 bytes) for each signature. So we get scalable quantum-safety for regular accounts, multisigs, etc. But it's only one specific signature scheme, you can't do anything else.

In leanSTARK, it's a STARK. This means it's fully general: the user runs whatever computation they want, and publish a STARK of it. So you can use it for:

* Any signature scheme (including eg. lattice-based ones if you like those)
* A multisig that hides its internal logic
* Privacy protocols
* Private account abstraction: authorization logic that depends on some value hidden elsewhere in the state, so you can have one key that controls all your accounts without publicly linking them to each other

Basically, it's a free for all, in the same way the EVM is a free for all.

But leanSTARK has a practical downside. The protocol would have to specify the language in which users write their programs (we call this the "ISA"). So we would have to agree on that language. This is a really big deal - it's the first big case of "Ethereum moving beyond the EVM" - and so it's likely to take time to agree on the details of it, especially since the ISA would be hard to upgrade. There are benefits to taking longer on this, figuring out the ideal ISA, and then even giving access to it inside regular contracts.

LeanPCS is the third option. PCS stands for "polynomial commitment scheme": a proof that P(x) = y. The most important thing to know about PCSes is that they are by far the most important "hard" component of a STARK (see here: https://t.co/EEQWMU0gAf ). If you have a "magic PCS oracle" (which from the EVM's point of view, 8288 is), you can verify a STARK in ~20-40k gas.

The most important gain with PCS is that there is far less that we need to choose. Specifying a PCS only requires specifying a field, and there is a natural option: the 128 bit binary field (technically, we can go more general than that, and say the 2^k-bit binary recursive tower field, going up to 256)

LeanPCS is less efficient than leanSTARK onchain, because you would have to put multiple claims to prove one thing. But it's arguably more efficient offchain, because you have much more flexibility to choose proof systems.

But most importantly, leanPCS gives you the same generality as leanSTARK, in a way that could potentially be implemented very quickly. And once we figure out the ISA, we can add leanSTARK later.

So there is a route to getting "the cryptographic proof singularity" much faster than any of us expected, and that route runs through 8288 with leanPCS.

So there is a route to getting "the cryptographic proof singularity" much faster than any of us expected, and that route runs through 8288 with leanPCS.
